title: 2025 DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development Report
author: DORA (Google Cloud)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report reinforces the cluster’s core claims that AI produces uneven gains, that value depends on organisational and workflow redesign rather than tool access alone, and that indiscriminate adoption is unwarranted. It materially extends the competence-risk proposition with cross-domain evidence from software development, highlighting tacit expertise transfer and recommending joint optimisation of productivity and skill development.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: DORA accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI gains are selective and depend on verification, user practices and workflow redesign. It materially extends that proposition with cross-domain organizational evidence linking outcomes to platform quality, value-stream management and seven enabling capabilities, while appropriately treating the survey associations as non-causal and software-specific.
qs: It magnifies the strengths of high- performing organizations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones.
AI adoption has a negligible effect on organizational performance when platform quality is low, but when platform quality is high, the effect is strong and positive.

kp.k: AI amplifies organizational strengths and weaknesses
kp.d: The report's central argument concerns software development, not legal services: AI's benefits depend on the surrounding technical and organizational system. It recommends treating adoption as organizational transformation rather than tool procurement, because faster individual work need not translate into organizational value.
qs: Key takeaway: AI is an amplifier
Successful AI adoption is a systems problem, not a tools problem

kp.k: Evidence combines survey comparisons and continuous qualitative research
kp.d: The survey, conducted June 13–July 21, 2025, received 4,867 responses, although conditionality and missingness mean not everyone entered every analysis. Researchers also interviewed 78 participants from July 2024–July 2025; 76 interviewees were in the U.S. Recruitment combined organic and panel channels. Survey respondents had a median age of 41 and median role experience of six years. These are observations of participants, not an experimental demonstration of AI's effects.
qs: a global survey conducted between June 13 and July 21, 2025
Not every respondent was part of each analysis because of survey conditionality or missingness.
These channels fall into two categories: organic and panel.

kp.k: Adoption estimates are observational, not established causal effects
kp.d: DORA measures AI adoption through trust, reliance and reflexive use, rather than usage alone. Its analysis uses exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, causal diagrams and targeted Bayesian models, reporting 89% credible intervals. The authors explicitly qualify causal language as comparisons dependent on assumptions. The methodology's worked numerical example uses simulated data and should not be mistaken for survey findings.
qs: Occasionally we will speak in causal terms, but ultimately, we’re doing comparisons.
Adoption is dynamic, but given we have a snapshot, we’re treating these highly co-determinant phenomena as unidimensional.
Generating fake data from our causal theory

kp.k: AI use is widespread but not invariably reflexive
kp.d: Ninety percent of respondents used AI at work, described as a 14.1% increase over the previous report's metric. AI users reported median experience of 16 months and median interaction time of two hours on their most recent workday. Among AI users, 7% always turned to AI for a problem or task, 27% did so most of the time, 26% about half the time and 39% sometimes. Sixty-five percent reported at least moderate reliance.
qs: AI user status
Reflexive AI use
General reliance on AI at work

kp.k: Code generation leads a broad task portfolio
kp.d: Among respondents who performed each task, 71% used AI for writing new code, 68% for literature reviews, 66% for modifying existing code, 64% for documentation, 62% for test cases, 59% for debugging and 56% for code review. These task-specific denominators matter: the figures do not describe the proportion of all respondents performing those activities with AI.
qs: Parenthetical is the % of all respondents who perform the task. The ‘Other’ category is excluded.

kp.k: Autonomous agents remain less common than conversational assistance
kp.d: Chatbots were used by 55% of respondents and IDE-based AI by 41%, compared with 18% for automated tool chains. Sixty-one percent reported never using agent mode, defined as relatively unsupervised operation that may change code without direct oversight. The authors suggest lower agent adoption reflects its more recent emergence, rather than establishing that explanation empirically.
qs: Where people interact with AI
Agent mode: AI autonomously operating in the background, possibly making changes without direct oversight

kp.k: Perceived gains coexist with limited trust
kp.d: More than 80% reported increased productivity; the displayed categories were 41% slightly, 31% moderately and 13% extremely increased. Fifty-nine percent perceived better code quality, while 30% saw no change. Thirty percent expressed little or no trust in AI-generated output: 23% a little and 7% none. DORA interprets this coexistence as compatible with useful assistance and recommends teaching critical guidance, evaluation and validation rather than merely encouraging usage.
qs: Perceived impact on individual productivity
Perceived impact on code quality
Trust in the quality of AI-generated output
This “trust but verify” approach is a sign of mature adoption.

kp.k: External experimental evidence challenges perceived productivity improvements
kp.d: The report separately cites METR's early-2025 experienced open-source developer study: developers slowed by 19% nevertheless believed AI made them 20% more efficient. DORA uses this external finding alongside its own positive self-reports to argue for realistic expectations and further evidence; the METR result is not a DORA survey estimate.
qs: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity.
a stark misalignment between perception and reality:

kp.k: Throughput improves while delivery instability remains associated with AI
kp.d: Higher AI adoption was associated with higher individual effectiveness, organizational performance, valuable work, code quality, product performance, delivery throughput and team performance, but similar burnout and friction and higher instability. Throughput and valuable work changed from negative associations in 2024 to positive in 2025; product performance changed from neutral to positive. The authors suggest adaptation by users, organizations and tools, while acknowledging that the survey cannot establish the mechanisms.
qs: • Similar levels of burnout
• Similar levels of friction
Changes in last year’s patterns suggest adaptation

kp.k: Faster delivery does not neutralize instability's harms
kp.d: The report tested whether AI adoption weakened instability's adverse relationships with outcomes and found no evidence of moderation. Instability remained detrimental to product performance and burnout. Strong delivery pipelines, testing, feedback and independence from other teams therefore remain important, although the authors leave open whether established engineering capabilities must evolve further.
qs: Some might argue that instability is an acceptable trade-off for the gains in development throughput that AI-assisted development enables.
We found no evidence of such a moderating effect.

kp.k: Verification and intensified expectations may absorb productivity gains
kp.d: DORA hypothesizes that friction shifts toward prompting, vetting results and checking plausible-looking code, while increased change volume can raise coordination and verification costs. Qualitative evidence also suggests that some organizations respond to perceived capacity gains by demanding more output and shortening timelines. These are proposed explanations for unchanged aggregate friction and burnout, not experimentally established mechanisms.
qs: prompt iteration, result vetting, and assessing code that looks remarkably similar to correct code.
Stakeholders are expecting more work to be done within [the product] in a quicker manner.

kp.k: Seven capabilities condition AI's organizational benefits
kp.d: From 15 candidate capabilities informed by interviews, expert discussion and prior research, DORA identifies seven with substantial evidence of interaction with AI adoption: clear communicated AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, AI-accessible internal data, strong version control, small batches, user-centric focus and quality internal platforms. This is an inaugural model intended for further validation and refinement, not a final universal prescription.
qs: These seven capabilities form the core of our new model:
As with the DORA Core Model,1 we will continue validating, revising, and refining the DORA AI Capabilities Model with further research.

kp.k: Policy clarity supports effective, bounded experimentation
kp.d: A clear AI stance was associated with stronger AI benefits for individual effectiveness and organizational performance and with reduced friction; evidence for throughput moderation was less certain. Interviews described both excessive caution and overly permissive use under unclear policies. The report says organizations should choose context-appropriate policies and communicate them, although its measure also includes encouragement, expectations and support for experimentation.
qs: Clarify and socialize your AI policies
Ambiguity around AI stifles adoption and creates risk.
Establish and socialize a clear policy on permitted tools and usage to build developer trust.

kp.k: Data quality and internal context have distinct benefits
kp.d: Healthy data ecosystems—quality, accessibility and reduced silos—amplified the association between AI adoption and organizational performance. AI access to internal company information separately amplified associations with individual effectiveness and code quality. The recommendation is to invest in secure integration with documentation, codebases and other internal sources rather than relying solely on generic models and purchased licenses.
qs: Treat your data as a strategic asset
Connect AI to your internal context
This means going beyond simply procuring licenses, and investing the engineering effort to give your AI tools secure access to internal documentation, codebases, and other data sources.

kp.k: Version control and small batches constrain risky acceleration
kp.d: Frequent commits amplified AI's association with individual effectiveness, while rollback practices amplified its association with team performance without directly reducing instability. Small batches strengthened product-performance benefits and reduced friction, but slightly attenuated perceived individual-effectiveness gains. DORA argues that product and organizational outcomes matter more than maximizing the perceived productivity of code generation.
qs: Embrace and fortify your safety nets
Reduce the size of work items
Instead, focus on outcomes.

kp.k: User focus distinguishes beneficial from harmful acceleration
kp.d: AI adoption was associated with better team performance under strong user-centric focus and worse performance when that focus was absent. The report recommends integrating users' needs, goals and feedback into product strategy: greater individual effectiveness can otherwise accelerate work in the wrong direction.
qs: Center users’ needs in product strategy
But, if their users’ needs aren’t their focus, they may be moving quickly in the wrong direction.

kp.k: Internal platforms support scaling but introduce trade-offs
kp.d: The report states that 90% of organizations had platforms, 76% had dedicated platform teams and 29% used multiple platforms. Platform quality strengthened AI's association with organizational performance but also increased friction for AI adopters, possibly through useful restrictions. Separately, quality platforms were associated with better performance and well-being alongside a small increase in delivery instability. The authors interpret the latter as potentially manageable risk compensation, rather than proof that instability is harmless.
qs: Platform adoption is nearly universal: 90%.
A platform should be seen as a holistic entity that enables a great developer experience.
Invest in your internal platform

kp.k: Value-stream management directs AI toward actual bottlenecks
kp.d: Teams reviewing and improving value streams reported higher team and product performance and more valuable work. Strong value-stream management also amplified AI's association with organizational performance. The practical mechanism is to map work from idea to customer, identify the binding constraint and target improvements there—for example, improving reviews instead of generating more code that accumulates in review queues.
qs: Value stream management (VSM) is the practice of visualizing, analyzing, and improving the flow of work from idea to customer.
Focus on flow, not just speed
Can we draw our software delivery value stream on a whiteboard?

kp.k: System redesign includes roles, incentives and governance
kp.d: In the AI mirror chapter, Eirini Kalliamvakou draws on systems thinking and the Theory of Constraints to distinguish augmenting existing workflows from designing AI-native ones. Recommendations include stronger review and deployment processes, contextual data integration, updated security controls and incentives for verification, delegation and orchestration. Agentic collaboration, swarming and Continuous AI are presented as emerging possibilities rather than established outcomes of the survey.
qs: Organizations are systems, not sums of individuals
Transformation in two ways: Augmenting and evolving
Rewarding behaviors like verification, delegation, prompt curation, and agent orchestration sends the right signals about what success looks like in an AI-accelerated environment.

kp.k: Seven team profiles broaden performance diagnosis
kp.d: Cluster analysis combined delivery throughput and instability with team and product performance, individual effectiveness, valuable work, friction and burnout. Profiles were foundational challenges (10%), legacy bottleneck (11%), constrained by process (17%), high impact/low cadence (7%), stable and methodical (15%), pragmatic performers (20%) and harmonious high-achievers (20%). The last two combined strong throughput and stability. Names and explanations are interpretations of clusters, not definitive diagnoses.
qs: The names and descriptions for each of these clusters are an interpretation of the data.
Look beyond software delivery performance

kp.k: Sociocognitive findings show limited disruption so far
kp.d: Higher AI adoption was associated with greater authentic pride, with valuable work offered as a mechanism. Researchers found no measurable relationships with meaningful work, need for cognition or existential connection. They reported 78% certainty against diminished ownership and a 21% probability of decreased ownership. AI adoption increased the perceived importance of prompt engineering and syntax memorization, but not the other six skills tested. The authors stress adaptation and uncertainty rather than concluding that longer-term effects are absent.
qs: Together, these findings indicate that AI adoption has not meaningfully impacted how developers experience their work lives.
Even as this technology becomes more autonomous, it is important for developers to see themselves as the ones in the driver’s seat.

kp.k: Automation may weaken apprenticeship while raising immediate output
kp.d: In a separate contribution, Matt Beane argues from research across more than 31 occupations and early software-engineering findings that expert self-service through automation can reduce novices' access to hands-on learning. He distinguishes productivity indicators from skill-development measures and recommends jointly optimizing both, including using AI to analyze developer interactions and version-control activity. This is Beane's research-based argument, not a measured DORA finding about junior displacement.
qs: Experts can self-serve, so they do.
Default AI usage patterns are delivering breakthrough productivity and blocking skill development for most devs.
Measuring and driving for both is the path to sustainable performance.

kp.k: Task demands influence whether assistance supports comprehension
kp.d: Edward Fraser reports a UC Berkeley eye-tracking and interview study of Python student developers with one to five years' experience completing two short tasks. AI chat received less than 1% visual attention during interpretation versus nearly 19% during more mechanical work. Participants sometimes ignored useful suggestions to retain understanding and control. The recommendation is task-sensitive customization, not assuming continuous assistance benefits every activity.
qs: Eye-tracking revealed less than 1% visual attention on AI chat during interpretive tasks, compared to nearly 19% during the more mechanical ones.
To reduce friction and better support focused work, developers and teams can customize their AI tools.

kp.k: Foreword cases illustrate conditional benefits, not survey estimates
kp.d: Gene Kim reports Adidas and Booking.com cases from his book with Steve Yegge. Adidas teams with loosely coupled architectures and fast feedback reported 20%–30% productivity gains and a 50% increase in Happy Time, whereas tightly coupled ERP teams saw little or no benefit. Booking.com reported up to 30% more merge requests after instruction and context training. These cases support the foreword's amplification hypothesis but are distinct from DORA's survey estimates.
qs: productivity gains of 20% to 30%, as measured by increases in commits, pull requests, and overall feature-delivery velocity,
50% increase in ‘Happy Time’
Fast feedback loops and software architecture

kp.k: Measurement should preserve outcomes and enable local experimentation
kp.d: The report recommends selecting frameworks such as DORA, SPACE, DevEx and HEART according to organizational goals, combining appropriate self-reports and logs, and adapting metrics rather than automatically replacing frameworks when AI arrives. It warns that both collection approaches have limitations. DORA delivery measures cover lead time, deployment frequency, failed-deployment recovery time, change failure rate and rework rate; longitudinal application-level improvement is preferred over simplistic ranking. Findings should inform locally tested hypotheses.
qs: They’re intended to get you closer to the truth, but you shouldn’t expect to measure everything.
Instrumentation approaches vary, errors can create inaccuracies, and interpretation is subject to bias.
Run experiments in your organization:

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: DORA presents AI as an amplifier of existing software-development capabilities, rather than a substitute for organizational improvement.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about software development, not legal services. DORA argues that AI's organizational benefits depend on technical foundations, workflows, and team alignment. Eirini Kalliamvakou's chapter develops this argument: faster coding does not necessarily improve delivery when testing, review, integration, deployment, or governance remain constraints. Her forecasts about organizational transformation are interpretations and recommendations grounded in the report, rather than independently demonstrated causal findings.

pts.k: AI use is widespread among surveyed software professionals, but autonomous agent use is much less common.
pts.d: Kevin M. Storer and Derek DeBellis report that 90% of respondents use AI at work. AI users report a median two hours of interaction on their most recent workday; 60% turn to AI about half the time or more when encountering a task or problem, and 65% rely on it a moderate amount or more. Among respondents whose work includes writing new code, 71% use AI for that task. Conversely, 61% report never interacting with AI in agent mode. The authors suggest lower agent adoption reflects its more recent emergence; this explanation is tentative. Agent mode means relatively unsupervised operation, not simply conversational assistance.

pts.k: Respondents perceive productivity and code-quality improvements while retaining reservations about AI output.
pts.d: Storer and DeBellis report that more than 80% perceive increased productivity and 59% perceive improved code quality. These are self-reported judgments, not measured time savings or independent code-quality assessments. Thirty percent express little or no trust in output quality, while 70% express at least some confidence. The authors argue that useful assistance can coexist with skepticism and recommend training in guiding and checking AI-generated work rather than merely encouraging adoption.

pts.k: Higher AI adoption is associated with better reported performance on several dimensions, but also greater delivery instability.
pts.d: DeBellis reports positive adjusted associations between AI adoption and individual effectiveness, organizational performance, valuable work, code quality, product performance, delivery throughput, and team performance. Burnout and friction show no measurable average relationship. Delivery instability increases. Relative to 2024, throughput and valuable work change from negative to positive associations, while product performance changes from neutral to positive. The proposed explanation—adaptation by users, organizations, and tool providers—is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated explanation of the year-to-year differences. The adoption measure combines trust, reliance, and reflexive use; it is not simply whether someone has an AI license.

pts.k: AI may relocate effort into verification and coordination, while increased output expectations can offset potential relief from burnout.
pts.d: DeBellis hypothesizes that manual production work can give way to prompting, vetting results, and checking plausible-looking code. Increased change volume may also raise coordination costs unless workflows and safeguards evolve. Qualitative interviews suggest that some employers respond to perceived capacity gains by expecting more output under tighter deadlines. These proposed mechanisms explain why perceived productivity gains need not reduce friction or burnout. The report also finds no evidence that AI adoption weakens the adverse relationship between delivery instability and outcomes such as product performance and burnout.

pts.k: The inaugural AI Capabilities Model identifies seven conditions associated with stronger benefits from AI adoption.
pts.d: Storer, DeBellis, and Nathen Harvey identify a clear and communicated AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, AI-accessible internal data, strong version control, small batches, user-centric focus, and quality internal platforms. Fifteen candidate capabilities were surveyed; seven showed substantial interaction evidence. Clear policy is associated with stronger effectiveness and organizational-performance benefits and reduced friction; throughput moderation is reported with less certainty. Healthy data strengthens the organizational-performance association, while internal context strengthens effectiveness and code-quality associations. Frequent commits strengthen effectiveness benefits, and rollback use strengthens team-performance benefits without directly reducing instability. These are observational interaction findings, notwithstanding stronger causal wording elsewhere in the report.

pts.k: The report identifies trade-offs: small batches can moderate individual gains while improving product outcomes; user focus determines whether team-level associations are beneficial.
pts.d: The AI Capabilities Model associates small batches with stronger product-performance benefits and reduced friction, but slightly smaller gains in self-reported individual effectiveness. The authors favor product outcomes over maximizing an individual's perceived productivity. They also report that AI adoption is associated with worse team performance where user-centric focus is absent and better performance where it is present. Quality platforms strengthen organizational-performance benefits but can increase friction for AI adopters; the proposed explanation is that platform guardrails constrain inappropriate uses.

pts.k: Platform quality and value stream management are presented as ways to convert individual AI gains into organizational benefits.
pts.d: Eric Maxwell and Benjamin Good report that the association between AI adoption and organizational performance is negligible with low-quality platforms and strong with high-quality platforms. Their forward-looking recommendation is to invest in platforms alongside AI. Rob Edwards reports that mature value stream management amplifies AI's organizational-performance association by directing improvements toward system-level constraints. His code-review example is illustrative: generating more code can worsen a review bottleneck, whereas improving review addresses the constraint. Separately, the platform chapter interprets a small increase in instability as potentially manageable when recovery is cheap and product performance remains strong; that conditional interpretation should not be conflated with evidence that AI makes instability harmless.

pts.k: The sociocognitive analysis finds greater authentic pride but limited evidence of broader changes in developers' experience of work.
pts.d: Daniella Villalba reports that higher AI adoption is associated with greater authentic pride, with valuable work offered as a mechanism. The analysis finds no measured relationship with meaningful work, need for cognition, or existential connection. It assigns 78% certainty to no association with diminished personal ownership and a 21% probability to decreased ownership. These are reported analytical probabilities, not percentages of developers who lost ownership. AI adoption increases the perceived importance of prompt engineering and syntax memorization but not the other examined skills. Villalba cautions against firm explanations and notes that some changes may be too early to detect.

pts.k: Contributor Matt Beane warns that default AI use can undermine apprenticeship even while raising productivity.
pts.d: Beane argues that senior staff can increasingly self-serve with automation, reducing novices' access to hands-on joint work and tacit learning. He bases this warning on research across more than 31 occupations and preliminary studies of AI use in software engineering since 2023, rather than a quantified result from the DORA survey. He recommends jointly measuring productivity and skill development and proposes using AI to analyze developer interactions and learning trajectories. His broad claim about blocked skill development should be attributed to him, not treated as the survey's finding.

pts.k: Kalliamvakou forecasts more central verification, orchestration, and workflow-design work, alongside emerging AI-native collaboration.
pts.d: Kalliamvakou proposes that delegating more development work to AI increases the importance of checking output, coordinating agents, and designing workflows. She describes potential AI-native pipelines, data maintenance, security response, agentic workflows, and swarming. These are prospective organizational possibilities, conditioned on appropriate data, integrations, monitoring, training, and incentives—not established evidence that autonomous systems have replaced developers. The report's current usage and ownership findings predominantly describe assistance rather than unsupervised substitution.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines observational survey analysis, interviews, attributed case studies, outside research, and contributor interpretation.
pts.d: The survey has 4,867 respondents, although conditional questions, missingness, and four randomized topic flows mean not all participated in every analysis. Recruitment combines organic and panel channels rather than a stated probability sample. Seventy-eight interviews provide more than 100 hours of qualitative material; 76 interviewees were in the United States. Outcomes are substantially self-reported. The report uses factor analysis, structural equation modeling, causal diagrams, and adjusted Bayesian comparisons, reporting 89% credible intervals. Its methodology's simulated coefficients and diagnostics illustrate an analytical workflow and are not empirical DORA findings. Additional evidence includes: Gene Kim's retelling of an Adidas pilot with 20–30% productivity gains and 50% more 'Happy Time' in teams with fast feedback and loosely coupled architecture, but little or no benefit under tight ERP coupling; his Booking.com example reporting up to 30% more merge requests after training; Edward Fraser's Berkeley student-developer study finding less than 1% attention to AI chat on interpretive tasks versus nearly 19% on mechanical tasks; and DeBellis's citation of METR's early-2025 experienced open-source developer study, reporting a 19% slowdown despite a perceived 20% improvement. These are distinct evidence sources, not DORA survey estimates. Sabre contributor Jacek Ostrowski separately reports 74% adoption, 86% perceived productivity improvement among users, and 25% uptake of agent mode.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe mid-2025 practice; future benefits and risks are conditional rather than dated forecasts.
pts.d: The global survey ran June 13–July 21, 2025; interviews ran July 2024–July 2025. Many adoption and experience questions cover the preceding three months, while some delivery questions cover six months and organizational performance covers the prior year. Comparisons with 2024 describe different annual findings, not tracked causal changes within a fixed panel. The seven-capability model is explicitly an inaugural framework awaiting further validation. Claims about stronger benefits depend on local technical and cultural conditions. The authors caution that widespread adoption does not justify immediate adoption by every organization and encourage context-specific experiments. They supply no fixed timetable for autonomous development, new roles, apprenticeship disruption, or workforce replacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern developers, software-delivery teams, organizational leaders, platform and security teams, novices, and software users.
pts.d: Developers may gain perceived effectiveness and more valuable work while assuming additional verification burdens and facing higher expectations. Junior staff may lose apprenticeship opportunities under Beane's account; experienced staff may self-serve more work. Delivery teams face possible improvements in throughput and product outcomes alongside greater instability. Leaders, platform teams, data engineers, and security professionals are asked to improve infrastructure, governance, internal context, and workflow constraints. End users benefit only insofar as faster production improves useful, reliable products. Survey participants span more than 100 countries and multiple organization sizes and industries, with technology, financial services, and retail/consumer/e-commerce prominent. The source does not establish changes in lawyer employment, law-firm staffing, legal pricing, legal markets, or access to justice.
